clue.text: Press flower delivered by vehicle

indicators.note: a speech is delivered out loud, so the word is taken by its spoken sound

blocks.note: a flower is something that flows, a river; the Forth is the Scottish river, and said out loud it matches the ordinal number
an estate is a British estate car, a station wagon

explanation.surface: Someone presses a flower that arrived by delivery van.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Flower' is crossword shorthand for a river (it flows); the Forth runs past Edinburgh. An estate is the British name for a station wagon.
explanation.definitionFit: The fourth estate is the established nickname for journalists and newspapers collectively, the press as a political power.

clue.text: Cool king’s mistress finally promoted soft soap

indicators.note: in a down entry, promotion moves something higher up the column, so the closing letter rises towards the top

blocks.note: a fan cools you
Nell Gwyn was mistress of King Charles II

explanation.surface: A calm monarch's lover, at last moving up in the world, deals in flattery.
explanation.walkthrough: Nell Gwyn, an orange-seller turned actress, is the classic royal mistress in crosswords. Flannel as flattery is British: a face flannel is a washcloth, hence the link with soap.
explanation.definitionFit: Flannel is British slang for flattering, evasive talk, just like soft soap meaning smooth persuasive praise.

clue.text: Country conserving excavated Lydian remains?

indicators.note: to excavate is to dig out the inside, leaving only the shell of the word
to conserve something is to keep it safely held within

blocks.note: the United Arab Emirates
the first and last letters of Lydian

explanation.surface: A modern nation preserves archaeological finds dug up from ancient Lydia.
explanation.walkthrough: The question mark flags that 'remains' means bones here, not ruins: ulnae are forearm bones, the kind of remains an excavation turns up.
explanation.definitionFit: Skeletal bones are what remains of a body after burial, and ulnae are forearm bones, so the plural fits by example.

clue.text: Turn on the Italian following singer in the night

indicators.note: what follows comes after, so the piece named first in the clue is placed second

blocks.note: a tit is a songbird
il is Italian for 'the'
late means far into the night

explanation.surface: An Italian man switches on the charm after hearing a singer at night.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Singer' is a bird, not a vocalist; 'following' places the Italian article after it.
explanation.definitionFit: To titillate is to excite or arouse someone pleasurably, which is what the slang phrase turn on means.

clue.text: Off-white bird with collar gutted for maiden

indicators.note: gutting removes the insides, so only the outermost letters remain
one thing in place of another, so a swap is being made

blocks.note: the large flightless Australian bird
the outside letters of collar
M is the cricket abbreviation for a maiden over

explanation.surface: A pale bird wears a plucked collar in place of a young girl.
explanation.walkthrough: The bird EMU has its M (maiden) replaced by CR, so it becomes E-CR-U.
explanation.definitionFit: Ecru is the pale greyish-yellow colour of unbleached linen, a shade usually described as off-white or beige.

clue.text: Lean on beam raised close to old jousting area

indicators.note: in a down entry, raising means reading from the bottom upwards
the close of a word is where it ends, so just its last letter is taken

blocks.note: to lean is to tilt
a beam of light is a ray
the last letter of old

explanation.surface: Someone leans on a raised beam beside the old tournament ground.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Old' looks like part of the definition, but only its closing letter is wanted. Tilting was jousting: riders charging each other with lances.
explanation.definitionFit: A tiltyard was the enclosed lists where knights tilted at each other with lances in medieval tournaments.

clue.text: American tailing pack in bay city

indicators.note: to tail is to follow close behind, so this piece is placed after the other

blocks.note: to tamp is to pack down firmly
A is a standard abbreviation for American

explanation.surface: An American follows a wolf pack around a city on the bay.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Tailing' means following behind, so the American's letter comes after the packing verb.
explanation.definitionFit: Tampa is a Florida city standing on Tampa Bay, on the Gulf coast, hence a city on a bay.

clue.text: Twinkling device lined with gold? One’s now available

indicators.note: something twinkling flickers and shifts restlessly, so the letters are rearranged
a lining sits inside a thing, so one piece goes within the other

blocks.note: taken as written
or is gold in heraldry

explanation.surface: A sparkling gadget with a gold lining is now on sale.
explanation.walkthrough: OR is the heraldic word for gold. 'Available' is about romance, not a shop: a divorced person is single again.
explanation.definitionFit: Someone who has divorced is unmarried again and therefore free to start a new romantic relationship.

clue.text: Too harassed essentially at the start of spring

indicators.note: the essence of something is its core, so only the central letters are kept

blocks.note: the two central letters of harassed
a spring is a well, a source of water

explanation.surface: Someone feels overly stressed when spring begins.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Spring' looks like the season but is a water source. 'At the start of' puts the first piece before it.
explanation.definitionFit: Too and as well are interchangeable adverbs meaning also or in addition, so they swap freely in a sentence.

clue.text: Relative catching adult runner by lake naked

indicators.note: to catch something is to take hold of it, so one piece ends up held inside

blocks.note: an aunt is a relative
A is the abbreviation for adult, as in film ratings
a runner is a river; the Ure is a Yorkshire river
L is the map abbreviation for lake

explanation.surface: A family member grabs a grown-up jogger, unclothed, beside a lake.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Runner' is a river, a crossword staple; the Ure flows through Yorkshire in northern England.
explanation.definitionFit: The French phrase au naturel is used in English to mean in a natural state, without clothes.

clue.text: Degrees incorporating popular courses

indicators.note: to incorporate is to take something into the body of a thing

blocks.note: Masters of Arts, plural
in means fashionable, popular

explanation.surface: University degrees that include well-attended courses of study.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Courses' looks academic beside 'Degrees', but it means parts of a meal.
explanation.definitionFit: Mains are main dishes, the central courses of a restaurant meal served after starters.

clue.text: Binning a quarter of unnecessary thread

indicators.note: throwing away a fourth of the word removes part of its letters

blocks.note: needless means unnecessary; its last two of eight letters form a quarter

explanation.surface: Discarding a quarter of some surplus thread.
explanation.walkthrough: The quarter removed is the final two letters of an eight-letter word.
explanation.definitionFit: To needle one's way is to thread through a narrow passage, weaving in and out as a sewing point does.

clue.text: US store rotated ornaments initially on tree

indicators.note: turning something round makes it face the other way, back to front
initially means at the beginning, so just the first letter

blocks.note: Macy's is the New York department store
first letter of ornaments
re means on the subject of, concerning

explanation.surface: An American shop turns its decorations round on a Christmas tree.
explanation.walkthrough: 'On' looks like a position word joining the pieces, but it supplies letters itself: RE, as in a memo's 'concerning'.
explanation.definitionFit: The sycamore is a large broad-leaved maple, a common deciduous tree in Britain and America.

clue.text: National network holding one in reserve

indicators.note: to hold something is to grip it inside, so one piece sits within another

blocks.note: a local area network in computing
the Roman numeral for one
as in 'put by' or 'by and by': set aside for later

explanation.surface: A national broadcasting network keeps one presenter on standby.
explanation.walkthrough: 'National' looks like an adjective about the network, but it is a noun: a citizen of a country. BY means aside, as in money put by.
explanation.definitionFit: A national is a citizen of a particular country, and a Libyan is a citizen of the North African state.

clue.text: Enjoyable snack for Spooner’s rowdy bash

indicators.note: the Reverend Spooner famously swapped the opening sounds of words, so the initial consonants trade places

blocks.note: an enjoyable snack is a fun bite; swapping the starting sounds gives the result

explanation.surface: A tasty nibble is laid on for a noisy party.
explanation.walkthrough: Swap the F and B of FUN BITE. A bunfight is British slang for a tea party or a heated squabble, originally a gathering where buns were served.
explanation.definitionFit: A bunfight is informally a lively, noisy gathering or a squabbling argument, matching a rowdy party or bash.

clue.text: Very hot current carrying queen

indicators.note: whatever carries a load holds it within, so one piece is placed inside the other

blocks.note: current affairs are topical ones, of present interest
R for Regina, Latin for queen

explanation.surface: A scorching electric current runs through the queen.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Current' suggests electricity or a river flow, but it is the adjective meaning up to date.
explanation.definitionFit: Tropical weather is the extreme heat and humidity found near the equator, so it describes something sweltering.

clue.text: Temple throne rebuilt in slate

indicators.note: rebuilding puts the materials together in a different arrangement
placing something in another means it sits inside it

blocks.note: taken as written
to slate a play is to pan it, criticise it harshly

explanation.surface: A temple's throne is reconstructed using slate stone.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Slate' looks like the roofing stone a builder would use, but it is the verb to criticise.
explanation.definitionFit: The Parthenon is the ancient Greek temple to Athena standing on the Acropolis in Athens.

clue.text: Electronic parts of fan above church disappear

indicators.note: in a down entry what sits above comes earlier, so the preceding pieces go first

blocks.note: E is the standard abbreviation for electronic, as in email
the blades of a fan are its vanes
the Church of England

explanation.surface: The electrical components of a ceiling fan over a church vanish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Parts of' looks like it might take some letters of fan, but it means the physical pieces of a fan.
explanation.definitionFit: To evanesce is a literary verb meaning to fade away gradually and vanish from sight, like vapour.

clue.text: Caught, formerly, by the setter’s grasp

indicators.note: by means next to, so the pieces are set side by side in order

blocks.note: c is the cricket scorecard abbreviation for caught
once means at some time in the past
the setter is 'I', and the setter's here is 'I've', I have

explanation.surface: A setter's catch from long ago, apparently still in their grip.
explanation.walkthrough: The apostrophe-s in 'setter's' is a contraction of 'has', not a possessive: the setter has, I've.
explanation.definitionFit: To conceive of an idea is to understand or form it in the mind, the mental sense of grasp.

clue.text: Funds keeping sailor up in African fortress

indicators.note: in a down entry, going up means reading from the bottom upwards, back to front
to keep something is to hold on to it within

blocks.note: cash is money, funds
AB, able seaman, is a sailor

explanation.surface: Money keeps a sailor going while stationed in a North African stronghold.
explanation.walkthrough: AB, for able-bodied seaman, is the usual crossword sailor.
explanation.definitionFit: A casbah is the walled citadel of a North African city, such as Algiers, so a fortified stronghold.

clue.text: Nick returning some shots erratically

indicators.note: some means a portion of, so the letters are a run inside the words that follow
to return is to go back the way you came, so the letters read backwards

blocks.note: the letters run across the end of the first word into the start of the second

explanation.surface: A goalkeeper saves some shots that come in wildly.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Erratically' looks like an anagram signal, but it is only fodder for the run of letters. Nick is British slang for arresting someone.
explanation.definitionFit: In British slang a policeman nicks a criminal, meaning arrests or apprehends them.

clue.text: Block steer periodically escaping across farm

indicators.note: if every other letter escapes, the ones left behind are spaced at regular intervals
something stretched across another spans it, holding it in between its ends

blocks.note: second and fourth letters of steer, the others having got away
a ranch is a large farm

explanation.surface: A steer keeps breaking out across the farm, so someone builds a barrier.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Block' looks like an obstruction for the escaping steer, but it is a noun for a portion.
explanation.definitionFit: A tranche is a portion or slice of something, such as a block of shares issued at one time.

clue.text: Close street prior to international launch

indicators.note: prior to means before, so what is named first comes earlier

blocks.note: the address abbreviation
I is a standard abbreviation for international
to fling is to hurl or launch something

explanation.surface: A road is shut ahead of a global product launch.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Close' reads as the verb to shut, but it is the adjective, as in close weather.
explanation.definitionFit: Close weather is humid and airless, and stifling heat is oppressively stuffy in just that way.

clue.text: Place briefly bolstered by male stand-in

indicators.note: something brief is cut short, so the word loses its last letter
a bolster props from beneath, so in a down entry the second piece sits below

blocks.note: locus is Latin for place, used in English for a site or position
M is the abbreviation for male

explanation.surface: A short-term post is propped up by a male substitute.
explanation.walkthrough: Locum is short for the Latin locum tenens, one holding the place, used chiefly of doctors and clergy.
explanation.definitionFit: A locum is a doctor or priest temporarily covering for another, a substitute filling in for a while.

clue.text: Fear over much prejudice on edges of parish

indicators.note: the edges of a word are its first and last letters
much of something is most but not all of it, so a letter is dropped
in an across entry one thing on another follows it, so the earlier pieces are placed after

blocks.note: the first and last letters of parish
O is the cricket scorebook abbreviation for an over
a bias is a prejudice

explanation.surface: Anxiety about too much bigotry at the fringes of a parish.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Over much' reads as excessive, but the two words split: one gives a letter and the other trims the next word.
explanation.definitionFit: A phobia is an irrational, intense dread of something specific, so a type of fear.

clue.text: Right to become tense in noble club

indicators.note: one thing becoming another means it is swapped out for something new

blocks.note: a baron is a nobleman
R is the abbreviation for right
T is the grammar abbreviation for tense

explanation.surface: A right to grow nervous inside an aristocrats' club.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Club' looks like a gentlemen's club for nobles, but it is a stick.
explanation.definitionFit: A baton is a short stick, such as a police truncheon, which is a type of club used as a weapon.

clue.text: Sandwich installing ordinary landscape eyesore?

indicators.note: installing something puts it in place inside a larger thing

blocks.note: a bacon, lettuce and tomato sandwich
O is the abbreviation for ordinary, as in the old British O level

explanation.surface: A sandwich bar is put up, spoiling an ordinary view.
explanation.walkthrough: The definition leans on the idiom 'a blot on the landscape', an ugly thing spoiling a view; the question mark admits it needs the phrase.
explanation.definitionFit: Something unsightly is called a blot on the landscape, a stain that spoils an otherwise pleasant view.

clue.text: For this purpose, supplement wine in auditorium

indicators.note: an auditorium is where an audience listens, so the words are taken by their sound

blocks.note: to supplement is to add; hock is a German white wine

explanation.surface: For the occasion, someone adds more wine in a concert hall.
explanation.walkthrough: Hock is the traditional British name for German Rhine wine. Ad hoc is Latin, literally 'to this'.
explanation.definitionFit: Ad hoc describes something arranged for a particular need only, which is the literal Latin meaning of the phrase.

clue.text: Peevish small student boring writer recalled quote

indicators.note: to bore is to drill into something, so one piece goes inside another
recalling calls something back, so the letters run backwards

blocks.note: S is the clothing abbreviation for small
a pen is a writing instrument
L for learner, as on a British learner driver's L-plate
to cite is to quote a source

explanation.surface: A crabby, undersized pupil bores a writer by repeating quotations.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Boring' looks like 'dull', but it means drilling into. 'Writer' is the instrument, not an author.
explanation.definitionFit: The spleen was once thought the seat of bad temper, so splenetic means irritable, bad-tempered and irascible.

clue.text: Tripe men cooked in nice runny sauce

indicators.note: cooking transforms raw ingredients into a new form
something runny has lost its shape and flows into a new one

blocks.note: taken as written
taken as written

explanation.surface: Butchers cook offal in a pleasant, runny sauce.
explanation.walkthrough: 'Sauce' looks culinary next to tripe, but it is British for cheek. Tripe is cow's stomach lining.
explanation.definitionFit: Sauce in British usage means cheeky insolence or rudeness, the same disrespectful boldness as impertinence.
